You are running an overnight autonomous development session on this
repository. Use the overnight-coordinator agent to manage the full session.
You have full permission to read, write, commit, push, and open draft PRs.
You do NOT have permission to merge to main or close PRs after opening them.

## SETUP (run once at session start)

```bash
# 1. Ensure we are on main and up to date
git checkout main
git pull

# 2. Rebuild the knowledge graph so you navigate current code, not stale code
# (only if graphify is installed — skip silently if not)
graphify update . --force 2>/dev/null || echo "graphify not installed — skipping"

# 3. Check for a prior checkpoint (resume if interrupted)
cat .claude/memory/checkpoint.md 2>/dev/null || echo "No checkpoint — starting fresh"

# 4. Read tonight's issues
gh issue list --label "ready-for-ai" --json number,title,body,labels \
  --order created --limit 20
```

If a checkpoint exists and shows IN PROGRESS or FAILED stages, resume
from there rather than starting over.

Write the session start to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
# Checkpoint
Session started: [timestamp]
Goal: Work through all ready-for-ai issues
Status: IN PROGRESS
Issues to process: [list from gh output]
Issues completed: []
Issues failed: []
Issues skipped: []
```

---

## FOR EACH ISSUE (in number order, lowest first)

### A. READ AND ASSESS

```bash
gh issue view [N] --comments
```

Ask: Is this issue clear enough to attempt autonomously?

**Blockers that cause a SKIP:**
- Requires a design decision not documented in the issue
- Depends on another issue that isn't complete yet
- Requires credentials, API keys, or external resources not available
- Scope is too vague to produce a verifiable result

If blocked, label and move on — do NOT guess at intent:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "needs-human" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Skipped overnight: [specific reason]. Please clarify before re-queuing."
```

### B. ORIENT

Invoke the git-historian agent:
"Use the git-historian agent to understand the code area this issue will touch."

This surfaces hot files, recent decisions, and things NOT to redo.
Read .claude/memory/history-brief.md after it completes.

### C. MARK IN PROGRESS

```bash
gh issue edit [N] --add-label "ai-in-progress" --remove-label "ready-for-ai"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Starting overnight implementation. Planning now."
```

### D. BRANCH

```bash
git checkout main
git checkout -b feature/issue-[N]
```

### E. PLAN

Use /plan-feature [concept from issue title] and wait for a plan.
Save the plan to .claude/plans/issue-[N].md

Do not implement until you have a written plan.

### F. IMPLEMENT

Use the appropriate specialist agents for this repo (see repo-specific
section below). Follow the plan. Write complete code — no placeholders.

If you hit a problem after 2 attempts on the same sticking point, SKIP
the issue and mark it ai-blocked. Do not spiral.

### G. TEST

Run the project's test suite. The exact commands are in the repo-specific
section below. Tests MUST pass before committing.

If tests fail after 2 fix attempts: skip, mark blocked, move on.
```bash
gh issue edit [N] --remove-label "ai-in-progress" --add-label "ai-blocked"
gh issue comment [N] --body "Blocked: tests failing after 2 attempts. [describe failure]. Needs human attention."
git checkout main
git branch -D feature/issue-[N]
```

### H. COMMIT AND PUSH

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "fix(#[N]): [issue title, shortened]"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### I. OPEN DRAFT PR

Generate the PR description using the /mr-description command, then:

```bash
gh pr create \
  --title "fix(#[N]): [issue title]" \
  --body "[output from /mr-description]" \
  --base main \
  --head feature/issue-[N] \
  --draft
```

Label the issue complete and close it with a reference to the PR:
```bash
gh issue edit [N] \
  --remove-label "ai-in-progress" \
  --add-label "ai-completed"
gh issue close [N] \
  --comment "Implemented. Draft PR open for review — see above."
```

### J. GENERATE LEARNING MATERIALS

**Identify the primary concept:**
Ask yourself: "What is the single most important technical concept a
developer would need to understand to maintain or extend this change?"

Guidelines:
- Choose the concept, not the feature name
  ("triple-channel SCPI addressing" not "E3631A support")
- Should be teachable in one lesson
- Should have testable recall in a drill
- Should introduce vocabulary worth learning

Then generate all three artifacts. In overnight/automated context:
- Generate the HTML files fully
- Skip in-chat interactive knowledge checks (no user present)
- Make the HTML content thorough — it is the only output
- Update PROGRESS.md with what was covered

```
/teach [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/drill-me [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/drills/NNNN-[concept].html

```
/terms [concept]
```
This creates docs/learning/vocab/NNNN-[concept].html
and updates docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md

Commit the learning materials on the same feature branch:
```bash
git add docs/learning/
git commit -m "docs(learning): add lesson, drill and vocab for [concept] (from issue #[N])"
git push origin feature/issue-[N]
```

### K. UPDATE CHECKPOINT

Append to .claude/memory/checkpoint.md:
```
Issue #[N]: [COMPLETED | FAILED | SKIPPED]
  Branch: feature/issue-[N]
  PR: #[PR number if opened]
  Concept taught: [concept]
  Learning files: lessons/NNNN-x.html, drills/NNNN-x.html, vocab/NNNN-x.html
  Notes: [anything notable]
```

Return to main: `git checkout main`

---

## END OF ALL ISSUES

### 1. Rebuild the learning index

```
/index
```

Commit:
```bash
git add docs/learning/index.html
git commit -m "docs(learning): rebuild index after overnight run $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
git push origin main
```

### 2. Write the morning report

Write OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md to the repo root:

```markdown
# Overnight Build Report
Date: [date]
Session duration: [start] to [finish]
Issues attempted: [N]

## Summary
[2-3 sentences on what was accomplished overall]

## Completed ✅
| Issue | Title | Branch | PR | Concept Taught |
|-------|-------|--------|----|----------------|
| #N | [title] | feature/issue-N | #PR | [concept] |

## Failed ❌
| Issue | Title | Failure Reason |
|-------|-------|----------------|
| #N | [title] | [why — specific, actionable] |

## Skipped (needs human) ⏭
| Issue | Title | Reason |
|-------|-------|--------|
| #N | [title] | [what needs clarification] |

## Learning Materials Created
| Concept | Lesson | Drill | Vocab |
|---------|--------|-------|-------|
| [concept] | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

## Test Status
[overall pass/fail and any notable failures]

## Suggested First Move
[The single most useful thing to do when you open your laptop]

## Draft PRs Awaiting Review
[list with PR numbers and one-line description each]
```

Commit and push the report:
```bash
git add OVERNIGHT_REPORT.md .claude/memory/checkpoint.md
git commit -m "chore: overnight report $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
git push origin main
```

---

## LEARNING CONCEPT SELECTION — GENERAL GUIDANCE

These guidelines apply to all repos unless overridden in a repo-specific
overnight-session command.

Choose a concept that:
- Is non-obvious (skip things any developer already knows)
- Will appear again in this codebase (worth learning for maintainability)
- Can be explained in one lesson without splitting into prerequisite lessons
- Has clear vocabulary (terms worth adding to the glossary)
- Produces useful recall questions in a drill

Avoid:
- Concepts named after specific model numbers or vendor names
  ("E3631A" is not a concept; "triple-channel PSU SCPI addressing" is)
- Concepts so generic they produce a useless lesson
  ("adding a class" — skip this)
- Concepts already well-covered in the existing lesson library
  (check docs/learning/PROGRESS.md first)

---

## FAILURE HANDLING POLICY

This policy applies to the entire session.

**Never stop the run because one issue failed.**
**Never silently skip — always label and comment.**
**Never attempt a risky or irreversible action without a prior commit.**

If at any point the session hits a situation that is genuinely ambiguous,
dangerous, or requires a human decision not covered by the issue:
1. Stop work on that issue
2. Label it needs-human
3. Leave a detailed comment explaining exactly what decision is needed
4. Move to the next issue

The goal is to maximize completed work, not to force through stuck issues.

---

## NOTE ON AUTOMATED LEARNING GENERATION

In a live session, /teach, /drill-me, and /terms end with in-chat
knowledge checks. In overnight autonomous mode, skip the interactive
questions and put that energy into making the HTML content more thorough
instead. The HTML is the deliverable — the in-chat conversation is not.

# Plan: Intraday Candlestick Strategy Engine (Engulfing v1)
Date: 2026-06-28
Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
Estimated complexity: L

## The Idea (one paragraph)
Add an intraday day-trading strategy layer to the existing algo trading platform,
starting with the Bullish/Bearish Engulfing pattern. The system downloads intraday
OHLCV bars (5-minute default) via yfinance, detects engulfing signals bar-by-bar, and
simulates trades with configurable position sizing, stop-loss, and take-profit on paper
money. A strategy base class makes it straightforward to add new candlestick or other
intraday patterns later without rewriting the simulation engine. Paper testing runs over
weeks or months of historical intraday data before any real-money connection is made.

## Goal
A user can run `intraday-sim --strategy engulfing --tickers AAPL,MSFT --interval 5m
--start 2026-01-01` and get a paper P&L report showing how the engulfing strategy
would have performed intraday, with per-trade log and equity curve CSV.

## Out of Scope (this version)
- Live / real-money execution (Robinhood connection for this strategy comes later)
- Intraday ML signal (the GBM model stays on daily bars for now)
- GUI or web UI integration (add after the CLI is validated)
- Anything under 5-minute bars (yfinance 1m data is only 7 days; 5m covers ~60 days)
- Combining engulfing signal with the existing GBM score (future work)
- Any second candlestick pattern beyond engulfing (designed for, not built)

"""Generate PWA app icon PNGs for the trading webapp.

Draws a candlestick chart motif on a dark navy background and exports three
sizes: 180×180 (iOS apple-touch-icon), 192×192, and 512×512 (PWA manifest).

Usage:
    python3 scripts/generate_icons.py
"""

import io
import pathlib

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as patches

OUTPUT_DIR = pathlib.Path(__file__).parent.parent / "webapp" / "static" / "icons"

BG_COLOR = "#111b2b"
FG_COLOR = "#ffffff"
TEAL = "#2fd4c4"
RED = "#e05c5c"
GREEN = "#4caf82"

SIZES = [
    ("icon-180.png", 180),
    ("icon-192.png", 192),
    ("icon-512.png", 512),
]


def draw_icon(size_px: int) -> bytes:
    """Return PNG bytes for the icon at the given pixel size."""
    dpi = 100
    fig_size = size_px / dpi

    fig = plt.Figure(figsize=(fig_size, fig_size), dpi=dpi)
    ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_facecolor(BG_COLOR)
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(BG_COLOR)

    pad = 0.12
    chart_left = pad
    chart_right = 1 - pad
    chart_bottom = pad + 0.08
    chart_top = 1 - pad

    # Three candlestick bars: red, red, green (engulfing)
    bars = [
        # (center_x, open_y, close_y, high_y, low_y, color)
        (0.28, 0.65, 0.50, 0.70, 0.45, RED),
        (0.50, 0.60, 0.45, 0.65, 0.40, RED),
        (0.72, 0.38, 0.72, 0.78, 0.33, GREEN),
    ]

    bar_half_width = 0.09

    for cx, open_y, close_y, high_y, low_y, color in bars:
        body_bottom = min(open_y, close_y)
        body_height = abs(close_y - open_y)

        # Wick (thin line through full high-low range)
        ax.plot(
            [cx, cx],
            [low_y, high_y],
            color=color,
            linewidth=max(1, size_px / 128),
            solid_capstyle="round",
        )

        # Body (filled rectangle)
        body = patches.FancyBboxPatch(
            (cx - bar_half_width, body_bottom),
            bar_half_width * 2,
            body_height,
            boxstyle="square,pad=0",
            linewidth=0,
            facecolor=color,
        )
        ax.add_patch(body)

    # Teal accent underline
    ax.plot(
        [chart_left, chart_right],
        [chart_bottom, chart_bottom],
        color=TEAL,
        linewidth=max(2, size_px / 80),
        solid_capstyle="round",
    )

    buf = io.BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format="png", dpi=dpi, facecolor=BG_COLOR)
    plt.close(fig)
    buf.seek(0)
    return buf.read()


def main() -> None:
    OUTPUT_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for filename, size in SIZES:
        out_path = OUTPUT_DIR / filename
        png_bytes = draw_icon(size)
        out_path.write_bytes(png_bytes)
        print(f"  wrote {out_path} ({size}×{size})")
    print("Done.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# mac-setup.sh — check prerequisites, start FastAPI server + ngrok tunnel,
# print the public URL, and clean up both processes on Ctrl-C.

set -euo pipefail

# ── Prerequisite checks ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Python >= 3.12
if ! python3 --version 2>/dev/null | grep -qE "3\.(1[2-9]|[2-9][0-9])"; then
    echo "ERROR: Python 3.12+ is required."
    echo "  Install from https://www.python.org/downloads/ or via Homebrew:"
    echo "  brew install python@3.12"
    exit 1
fi

# uv
if ! command -v uv >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "ERROR: uv is not installed."
    echo "  Install uv: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh"
    exit 1
fi

# ngrok
if ! command -v ngrok >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "ERROR: ngrok is not installed."
    echo "  Install ngrok: brew install ngrok/ngrok/ngrok"
    echo "  OR download from: https://ngrok.com/download"
    exit 1
fi

# Port 8000
if lsof -ti:8000 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    PID_ON_PORT=$(lsof -ti:8000)
    echo "ERROR: Port 8000 is already in use by PID ${PID_ON_PORT}."
    echo "  Run: kill ${PID_ON_PORT}   then retry."
    exit 1
fi

# Optional .env file
if [ -f .env ]; then
    # shellcheck disable=SC1091
    source .env
fi
if [ -z "${WEB_AUTH_USER:-}" ]; then
    echo "WARNING: WEB_AUTH_USER not set — server will start without authentication."
fi

# ── Install Python dependencies ────────────────────────────────────────────────

echo "Installing dependencies..."
uv sync --quiet 2>/dev/null || pip install -e . -q

# ── Start FastAPI server in background ────────────────────────────────────────

echo "Starting FastAPI server on http://127.0.0.1:8000 ..."
uv run uvicorn webapp.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 &
SERVER_PID=$!

# Wait up to 5 s for port 8000 to accept connections
READY=0
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
    if nc -z 127.0.0.1 8000 2>/dev/null; then
        READY=1
        break
    fi
    sleep 0.5
done

if [ "$READY" -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "ERROR: FastAPI server did not start within 5 seconds."
    kill "$SERVER_PID" 2>/dev/null || true
    exit 1
fi

# ── Start ngrok tunnel in background ──────────────────────────────────────────

echo "Starting ngrok tunnel..."
ngrok http 8000 --log=stdout >/tmp/ngrok.log 2>&1 &
NGROK_PID=$!

# Poll ngrok local API for the public URL (up to 10 s)
PUBLIC_URL=""
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
    PUBLIC_URL=$(curl -s http://127.0.0.1:4040/api/tunnels 2>/dev/null \
        | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d['tunnels'][0]['public_url'])" \
        2>/dev/null || true)

# Mac Setup Guide — AlgoTrade on iPhone

Run the trading webapp on your Mac and access it from your iPhone via a free ngrok tunnel.

---

## Prerequisites

Install these once before your first run.

**Python 3.12+**
Download from [python.org/downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/) or via Homebrew:
```bash
brew install python@3.12
```

**uv** (fast Python package manager)
```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

**ngrok** (reverse tunnel — required for the iPhone to reach your Mac)
```bash
brew install ngrok/ngrok/ngrok
```
OR download from [ngrok.com/download](https://ngrok.com/download).

**ngrok free account** — required for HTTPS tunnels.
Sign up at [ngrok.com](https://ngrok.com) (free tier is enough). After signing up, authenticate your local ngrok install:
```bash
ngrok config add-authtoken YOUR_TOKEN
```
HTTPS is required because iOS Safari will not install a PWA from a plain `http://` URL.

---

## Clone and first-time setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/bjl14710/algo_trading_practice.git
cd algo_trading_practice
chmod +x mac-setup.sh
```

---

## Running the app

```bash
./mac-setup.sh
```

What each step in the output means:

| Output line | What is happening |
|-------------|-------------------|
| `Installing dependencies...` | `uv sync` is downloading the Python packages listed in `pyproject.toml` |
| `Starting FastAPI server on http://127.0.0.1:8000` | The web app is starting in the background; only reachable locally |
| `Starting ngrok tunnel...` | ngrok is opening a secure tunnel from the internet to your local port 8000 |
| `✅  Server: http://127.0.0.1:8000` | The local server is ready |
| `🌐  Public: https://abc123.ngrok-free.app` | This is the URL your iPhone opens |
| `📱  Open the public URL on your iPhone...` | Prompt to install the home screen shortcut |
| `Press Ctrl-C to stop.` | The script is now holding both processes alive |

---

## Adding to iPhone home screen

Open the printed `https://...ngrok-free.app` URL on your iPhone. Then:

1. **Open Safari** on your iPhone. (You must use Safari — Chrome on iOS cannot install PWAs.)
2. **Navigate** to the printed ngrok URL.
3. **Tap the Share button** — the rectangle with an arrow pointing up, located in the centre of the bottom toolbar in Safari.
4. **Scroll down** in the share sheet and tap **"Add to Home Screen"**.
5. **Edit the name** if you like — it defaults to "AlgoTrade".
6. Tap **"Add"** in the upper-right corner.
7. The AlgoTrade icon now appears on your home screen. Tap it to open the app full-screen with no browser toolbar.

---

## Daily use

- **Your Mac must be awake** and `./mac-setup.sh` must be running for the iPhone to reach the app.
- **The ngrok URL changes every time you restart the script** (free tier limitation). If you stop and restart the script, open the new URL in Safari and re-add it to your home screen — or just use Safari to navigate to the new URL.

- **To keep your Mac awake while the script runs:**
  ```bash
  caffeinate -i ./mac-setup.sh
  ```
  This prevents the Mac from sleeping while the command is running.

---

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| `"Port 8000 already in use"` | Run `lsof -ti:8000 \| xargs kill` then retry |
| `"ngrok is not installed"` | Run `brew install ngrok/ngrok/ngrok` |
| `"Python 3.12+ is required"` | Install Python 3.12 from python.org or `brew install python@3.12` |
| iPhone shows `"Safari cannot open the page"` | Mac is asleep or `./mac-setup.sh` is not running |

| App works at home but not away | The tunnel is up but your Mac may be sleeping — use `caffeinate -i ./mac-setup.sh` |

Lesson 0034 · Web Platform

Progressive Web Apps & iOS Installation

Why the AlgoTrade webapp can live on your iPhone home screen — without the App Store.

1 · What Is a PWA and Why Does It Matter Here?

A Progressive Web App (PWA) is a regular website that the browser can install as if it were a native app. On iOS, the user taps "Add to Home Screen" in Safari and the app gets an icon, a splash screen, and — crucially — launches without the Safari URL bar (called "standalone" mode). The user experience is indistinguishable from a native app for simple tools like the AlgoTrade dashboard.

The AlgoTrade webapp at webapp/ is a FastAPI server. It already runs in a browser. Adding PWA support required exactly four things:

  1. App icon PNGs at the right sizes (webapp/static/icons/)
  2. A Web App Manifest JSON file (webapp/static/manifest.json)
  3. iOS-specific <meta> tags in base.html
  4. An HTTPS URL (provided by ngrok)
Why this matters for algo trading: The dashboard is running on a Mac at home. ngrok exposes it over HTTPS. You tap an icon on your phone and see your live positions — no App Store review, no $99 developer account, no cloud server required during the prototyping phase.

2 · The HTTPS Requirement — Secure Contexts

iOS Safari will not install a PWA from a plain http:// URL. This is the Secure Context requirement baked into the browser.

What is a Secure Context?

A secure context is a browsing context in which the browser considers the content to have been delivered securely. The rules:

  • https:// — always a secure context (TLS encrypts the connection)
  • http://localhost and http://127.0.0.1 — treated as secure by most browsers (local loopback)
  • http:// on any other host — not a secure context

PWA installation (the "Add to Home Screen" prompt) is gated on secure context. So is a growing list of browser APIs: geolocation, camera, notifications, service workers, clipboard write.

Why ngrok solves this

Your Mac's local server is at http://127.0.0.1:8000 — a secure context for your Mac's browser. But your iPhone connects over cellular to the Mac's private IP, which is a plain http:// non-loopback address — not a secure context for the iPhone.

ngrok creates a reverse tunnel: ngrok's servers accept HTTPS connections from the internet and forward them over an encrypted tunnel to http://127.0.0.1:8000 on your Mac. The iPhone sees a valid https://abc123.ngrok-free.app URL — secure context, PWA install unlocked.

## Without ngrok (broken for PWA on iPhone)

iPhone ──(cellular)──→ http://192.168.1.10:8000   ✗ Not HTTPS
                        ↳ "Add to Home Screen" greyed out

## With ngrok (works)

iPhone ──(cellular)──→ https://abc123.ngrok-free.app
                        ↓ (ngrok tunnel, encrypted)
                        → http://127.0.0.1:8000  (your Mac)
                        ✓ Secure context → PWA install enabled
How ngrok's tunnel works: When you run ngrok http 8000, ngrok's client opens a persistent TCP connection to ngrok's servers. The server then routes incoming HTTPS requests through that connection to your local port. Your Mac never needs a public IP or open firewall port — the Mac initiated the outbound connection.

3 · The Web App Manifest

The Web App Manifest is a JSON file that tells the browser how to present the app when installed. It lives at a static URL and is linked from the HTML <head>.

The manifest we created

// webapp/static/manifest.json
{
  "name":             "Algo Trader",      // full name in splash screen
  "short_name":        "AlgoTrade",        // label under home screen icon
  "display":           "standalone",       // no browser chrome when launched
  "start_url":         "/",                // page opened when icon is tapped
  "background_color":  "#111b2b",          // splash screen background
  "theme_color":       "#111b2b",          // status bar tint on Android
  "icons": [
    { "src": "/static/icons/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/static/icons/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
  ]
}

Key fields explained

FieldEffectNotes
displayControls browser chrome visibilitystandalone = no URL bar. Other values: browser, minimal-ui, fullscreen
short_nameText under the home screen iconKeep ≤12 chars or iOS truncates it
start_urlPage opened on launch/ means root; could be /dashboard
theme_colorAndroid status bar tint; Chrome tab stripeiOS ignores this — use the apple meta tags instead
background_colorSplash screen while app loadsShould match your app's main background
iconsIcon used by Android Chrome and PWA installiOS ignores this — uses the apple-touch-icon link instead

Linking the manifest from HTML

<!-- webapp/templates/base.html -->
<link rel="manifest"
      href="{{ url_for('static', path='/manifest.json') }}">
<!-- url_for generates the correct path even if the app is mounted
     at a subdirectory; never hardcode /static/... -->

4 · iOS-Specific Meta Tags

Apple implemented home screen web apps before the W3C Manifest spec existed — which means iOS Safari has its own proprietary tags that parallel (but don't replace) the manifest. You need both.

<!-- Standard PWA (Chrome/Android reads this) -->
<link rel="manifest" href="/static/manifest.json">

<!-- iOS-specific: enables standalone mode on Safari -->
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes">

<!-- iOS status bar appearance: black, black-translucent, or default -->
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style"
      content="black-translucent">

<!-- Name shown under the icon and on the splash screen -->
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-title" content="AlgoTrade">

<!-- The icon iOS actually uses — 180×180 for modern iPhones -->
<link rel="apple-touch-icon"
      href="{{ url_for('static', path='/icons/icon-180.png') }}">

<!-- Without this, mobile browsers render a 980px-wide desktop page -->
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

What each tag does

TagWhat it controlsWithout it
apple-mobile-web-app-capable: yesEnables full-screen standalone mode on launchApp opens in Safari with URL bar (not standalone)
apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-styleiOS status bar appearance when in standalone modeDefault grey status bar (clashes with dark UI)
apple-mobile-web-app-titleLabel under the home screen iconiOS uses the page <title>, which may be too long
apple-touch-iconPNG used as the home screen icon on iOSiOS screenshots the page and uses that as the icon (ugly)
viewportTells the browser to use the device's real widthPage renders zoomed out to 980px — text is tiny
iOS ignores the manifest icons array. Android Chrome reads manifest.json → icons. iOS Safari reads only the <link rel="apple-touch-icon"> tag. This is why we have both: icon-180.png (iOS) and icon-192.png / icon-512.png (Android/Chrome).

5 · Icon Sizes — Why Three?

Icons at different pixel densities serve different use cases:

FileSizeUsed byWhy this size
icon-180.png180×180iOS apple-touch-iconiPhone Retina @3× (60pt icon × 3px/pt). Used for home screen, multitasking, Spotlight.
icon-192.png192×192Android Chrome PWA manifestMinimum size Chrome requires for "Add to Home Screen" prompt
icon-512.png512×512Android splash screen; PWA storesUsed when Chrome shows the app's launch splash screen; also required by some PWA audits

How we generate them from code

scripts/generate_icons.py uses matplotlib (already a project dependency) to draw the icon and export all three sizes. No design tools, no Photoshop, no new packages:

def draw_icon(size_px: int) -> bytes:
    dpi = 100
    fig = plt.Figure(figsize=(size_px / dpi, size_px / dpi), dpi=dpi)
    ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])   # fill the entire figure
    ax.set_facecolor("#111b2b")           # dark navy background
    # ... draw candlestick bars ...
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format="png")       # in-memory export
    return buf.getvalue()

# Regenerate at any time with: python3 scripts/generate_icons.py
Key technique: fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1]) removes all margin (the default matplotlib figure has padding around the axis). This lets us treat the entire PNG canvas as the icon, with no whitespace around the art.

6 · PWA vs Native App — What's the Same, What Differs

PWA (what we built)

  • No App Store — install directly from Safari
  • No Apple Developer account ($0)
  • Updates instantly: refresh the page
  • Same codebase as the desktop site
  • Limited access to device APIs (no push notifications on older iOS, no background sync)
  • Requires the server to be running and reachable
  • Launched standalone (display: standalone in manifest)

Native App (e.g. Swift / React Native)

  • Distributed via App Store (requires $99/yr account and review)
  • Works offline (assets bundled in the binary)
  • Full access to device hardware and OS APIs
  • Must pass App Store review for each update
  • Separate codebase from the web version
  • Installed from a .ipa or .apk binary, not a URL

For the AlgoTrade dashboard: a PWA is the right choice right now. The app is data-heavy and UI-light. The server must be running for the data to be live anyway, so offline mode adds no value. And we bypass the App Store entirely.

7 · Quiz

5 questions. Click an answer to see the explanation.

1. Why does iOS Safari refuse to install a PWA from http://192.168.1.10:8000?

  • The address is not a secure context — only HTTPS or localhost qualify
  • Safari doesn't support PWAs at all
  • Port 8000 is blocked on iOS — only port 443 works
  • Apple blocks access to private IP addresses from Safari

2. The manifest has "display": "standalone". What does this change compared to the default?

  • The app can now access the camera and microphone
  • The app opens without a URL bar or Safari navigation controls
  • The app works offline because assets are cached automatically
  • The app takes over the full screen including the status bar area

3. iOS Safari reads icon sources from which tag?

  • manifest.json → "icons" array
  • <link rel="icon"> (favicon)
  • <link rel="apple-touch-icon">
  • <meta property="og:image">

4. ngrok starts with ngrok http 8000. Which statement best describes how the tunnel works?

  • ngrok opens a firewall port on your Mac and gives it a public IP
  • ngrok creates a VPN between your iPhone and your Mac
  • The ngrok client opens an outbound TCP connection to ngrok's servers, which forward incoming HTTPS requests back through it to localhost:8000
  • ngrok assigns your Mac a permanent static HTTPS subdomain

5. Which meta tag prevents iOS Safari from zooming in when the user taps a form input?

  • apple-mobile-web-app-capable
  • theme-color
  • viewport with initial-scale=1
  • CSS font-size: 16px on input, select, and textarea

8 · Scenario Check

Scenario A: You restart mac-setup.sh and the ngrok URL changes. Your iPhone's home screen icon stops working. What's the cheapest fix?

Answer: Open the new URL in Safari and tap "Add to Home Screen" again to create a second icon, or navigate via Safari to the new URL to update the browser's memory of the app. (ngrok paid tiers allow a static subdomain — but for now, just re-share the URL.)
Scenario B: A teammate adds a new page at /signals. They want the PWA to open that page instead of / when launched from the home screen icon. Where exactly do they change this?

Answer: Change "start_url": "/" to "start_url": "/signals" in webapp/static/manifest.json. The user must re-add the app to their home screen to pick up the change (the manifest is cached).
Scenario C: The webapp is now served at https://myapp.example.com/algo/ (a subdirectory). The icons at /static/icons/icon-180.png return 404. What's broken and how do you fix it?

Answer: The hardcoded /static/... absolute path doesn't account for the subdirectory mount. Use FastAPI's url_for('static', path='/icons/icon-180.png') in base.html — it generates the correct path relative to the app's mount point. The manifest.json icons array uses absolute paths; update those to /algo/static/icons/... or use a server-side template to generate them.

start_urlPage opened on launch/ means root; could be /dashboard
theme_colorAndroid status bar tint; Chrome tab stripeiOS ignores this — use the apple meta tags instead

Linking the manifest from HTML

<!-- webapp/templates/base.html -->
<link rel="manifest"
      href="{{ url_for('static', path='/manifest.json') }}">
<!-- url_for generates the correct path even if the app is mounted
     at a subdirectory; never hardcode /static/... -->

4 · iOS-Specific Meta Tags

Apple implemented home screen web apps before the W3C Manifest spec existed — which means iOS Safari has its own proprietary tags that parallel (but don't replace) the manifest. You need both.

<!-- Standard PWA (Chrome/Android reads this) -->
<link rel="manifest" href="/static/manifest.json">

<!-- iOS-specific: enables standalone mode on Safari -->
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-capable" content="yes">

<!-- iOS status bar appearance: black, black-translucent, or default -->
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style"
      content="black-translucent">

<!-- Name shown under the icon and on the splash screen -->
<meta name="apple-mobile-web-app-title" content="AlgoTrade">

<!-- The icon iOS actually uses — 180×180 for modern iPhones -->
<link rel="apple-touch-icon"
      href="{{ url_for('static', path='/icons/icon-180.png') }}">

<!-- Without this, mobile browsers render a 980px-wide desktop page -->
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

What each tag does

TagWhat it controlsWithout it
apple-mobile-web-app-capable: yesEnables full-screen standalone mode on launchApp opens in Safari with URL bar (not standalone)
apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-styleiOS status bar appearance when in standalone modeDefault grey status bar (clashes with dark UI)
apple-mobile-web-app-titleLabel under the home screen iconiOS uses the page <title>, which may be too long
apple-touch-iconPNG used as the home screen icon on iOSiOS screenshots the page and uses that as the icon (ugly)
viewportTells the browser to use the device's real widthPage renders zoomed out to 980px — text is tiny
iOS ignores the manifest icons array. Android Chrome reads manifest.json → icons. iOS Safari reads only the <link rel="apple-touch-icon"> tag. This is why we have both: icon-180.png (iOS) and icon-192.png / icon-512.png (Android/Chrome).

5 · Icon Sizes — Why Three?

Icons at different pixel densities serve different use cases:

FileSizeUsed byWhy this size
icon-180.png180×180iOS apple-touch-iconiPhone Retina @3× (60pt icon × 3px/pt). Used for home screen, multitasking, Spotlight.
icon-192.png192×192Android Chrome PWA manifestMinimum size Chrome requires for "Add to Home Screen" prompt
icon-512.png512×512Android splash screen; PWA storesUsed when Chrome shows the app's launch splash screen; also required by some PWA audits

How we generate them from code

scripts/generate_icons.py uses matplotlib (already a project dependency) to draw the icon and export all three sizes. No design tools, no Photoshop, no new packages:

def draw_icon(size_px: int) -> bytes:
    dpi = 100
    fig = plt.Figure(figsize=(size_px / dpi, size_px / dpi), dpi=dpi)
    ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])   # fill the entire figure
    ax.set_facecolor("#111b2b")           # dark navy background
    # ... draw candlestick bars ...
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format="png")       # in-memory export
    return buf.getvalue()

# Regenerate at any time with: python3 scripts/generate_icons.py
Key technique: fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1]) removes all margin (the default matplotlib figure has padding around the axis). This lets us treat the entire PNG canvas as the icon, with no whitespace around the art.

6 · PWA vs Native App — What's the Same, What Differs

PWA (what we built)

  • No App Store — install directly from Safari
  • No Apple Developer account ($0)
  • Updates instantly: refresh the page
  • Same codebase as the desktop site
  • Limited access to device APIs (no push notifications on older iOS, no background sync)
  • Requires the server to be running and reachable
  • Launched standalone (display: standalone in manifest)

Native App (e.g. Swift / React Native)

  • Distributed via App Store (requires $99/yr account and review)
  • Works offline (assets bundled in the binary)
  • Full access to device hardware and OS APIs
  • Must pass App Store review for each update
  • Separate codebase from the web version
  • Installed from a .ipa or .apk binary, not a URL

For the AlgoTrade dashboard: a PWA is the right choice right now. The app is data-heavy and UI-light. The server must be running for the data to be live anyway, so offline mode adds no value. And we bypass the App Store entirely.

7 · Quiz

5 questions. Click an answer to see the explanation.

1. Why does iOS Safari refuse to install a PWA from http://192.168.1.10:8000?

  • The address is not a secure context — only HTTPS or localhost qualify
  • Safari doesn't support PWAs at all
  • Port 8000 is blocked on iOS — only port 443 works
  • Apple blocks access to private IP addresses from Safari

2. The manifest has "display": "standalone". What does this change compared to the default?

  • The app can now access the camera and microphone
  • The app opens without a URL bar or Safari navigation controls
  • The app works offline because assets are cached automatically
  • The app takes over the full screen including the status bar area

3. iOS Safari reads icon sources from which tag?

  • manifest.json → "icons" array
  • <link rel="icon"> (favicon)
  • <link rel="apple-touch-icon">
  • <meta property="og:image">

4. ngrok starts with ngrok http 8000. Which statement best describes how the tunnel works?

  • ngrok opens a firewall port on your Mac and gives it a public IP
  • ngrok creates a VPN between your iPhone and your Mac
  • The ngrok client opens an outbound TCP connection to ngrok's servers, which forward incoming HTTPS requests back through it to localhost:8000
  • ngrok assigns your Mac a permanent static HTTPS subdomain

5. Which meta tag prevents iOS Safari from zooming in when the user taps a form input?

  • apple-mobile-web-app-capable
  • theme-color
  • viewport with initial-scale=1
  • CSS font-size: 16px on input, select, and textarea

8 · Scenario Check

Scenario A: You restart mac-setup.sh and the ngrok URL changes. Your iPhone's home screen icon stops working. What's the cheapest fix?

Answer: Open the new URL in Safari and tap "Add to Home Screen" again to create a second icon, or navigate via Safari to the new URL to update the browser's memory of the app. (ngrok paid tiers allow a static subdomain — but for now, just re-share the URL.)
Scenario B: A teammate adds a new page at /signals. They want the PWA to open that page instead of / when launched from the home screen icon. Where exactly do they change this?

Answer: Change "start_url": "/" to "start_url": "/signals" in webapp/static/manifest.json. The user must re-add the app to their home screen to pick up the change (the manifest is cached).
Scenario C: The webapp is now served at https://myapp.example.com/algo/ (a subdirectory). The icons at /static/icons/icon-180.png return 404. What's broken and how do you fix it?

Answer: The hardcoded /static/... absolute path doesn't account for the subdirectory mount. Use FastAPI's url_for('static', path='/icons/icon-180.png') in base.html — it generates the correct path relative to the app's mount point. The manifest.json icons array uses absolute paths; update those to /algo/static/icons/... or use a server-side template to generate them.
